patients.summary: Self-employed landscaper who joins in 2019 with peptic ulcer disease on pantoprazole, develops hypertension that becomes resistant with hypokalemia, and is found to have primary aldosteronism. A functioning pancreatic VIPoma is found in 2024 and resected; a vomiting ED visit in 2025 and a basilar tip aneurysm rupture in 2026 follow, with spironolactone finally added at her last visit.

documents.title: New Patient Preventive Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
41F here to establish care. Prior PCP retired; records requested.

Concerns: none really. Feels well. Works outdoors all season, slower in winter.

PMH: peptic ulcer disease about 7 yrs ago, treated at her old office; has stayed on pantoprazole 40 daily since and doesn't want to come off it ("every time I tried, the burning came back"). Diagnostic laparoscopy at 32 for abdominal pain, nothing found.
Meds: pantoprazole 40 mg daily. No OTC NSAIDs - was told to avoid after the ulcer.
Allergies: NKDA.
FHx: father HTN, died after a ruptured brain aneurysm at 67. Mother T2DM and high cholesterol. Paternal aunt has an adrenal problem causing high BP - pt thinks it was called hyperaldosteronism.
SHx: self-employed landscaper/horticulturist, runs a small crew in season. Never smoker. Wine 1-2 glasses a month. Exercises through work.
GYN: regular cycles. Last Pap "a few years ago," normal. No mammogram yet.

ROS: no headaches, chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, abdominal pain, change in bowels, melena. Otherwise negative.

Exam: BP above, repeated after rest similar. Pleasant, fit-appearing, tanned forearms. HEENT normal. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, healed laparoscopy port scars. No edema. Skin: no concerning lesions on sun-exposed areas. Pelvic: normal external genitalia, cervix normal, Pap/HPV collected. Breasts: no masses bilaterally.

A/P
1. Health maintenance: Pap/HPV done. Screening mammogram ordered. Tdap today. CMP, CBC, lipids, TSH, A1c. One-time HCV and HIV screening, discussed and agreed.
2. BP borderline today. With her father's history I'd like real numbers - asked her to buy a home cuff and send readings over the next couple months. Low salt diet reviewed.
3. PUD hx - continue pantoprazole. Avoid NSAIDs.
4. FHx of ruptured aneurysm in father - noted.
RTC 1 yr, sooner for BP.

documents.title: Endocrinology Consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE ENDOCRINOLOGY - CONSULTATION LETTER
Date of visit: 03/21/2022
Referred by primary care for resistant hypertension with hypokalemia.

Thank you for asking us to see Ms. Nowak, a 44-year-old landscaper. For roughly half a year her headaches have been getting worse and she has felt more tired, with muscle weakness at the end of the workday. She also describes occasional spells of a racing heart with sweating. Hypertension was first diagnosed about two years ago and has never been well controlled despite an ACE inhibitor, a calcium channel blocker and a thiazide.

Medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, potassium chloride 40 mEq twice daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
PMH: peptic ulcer disease. PSH: diagnostic laparoscopy at 32, negative.
Family history: father with hypertension who died of a ruptured cerebral aneurysm at 67; mother with type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia; paternal aunt with primary hyperaldosteronism.
Social: never smoker; wine once or twice a month; self-employed in landscaping and horticulture.

Exam: BP 158/100. Comfortable. No cushingoid features. Heart regular. No abdominal bruits. No edema.

Labs today: sodium 145 mEq/L, potassium 3.1 mEq/L on replacement. Plasma aldosterone concentration elevated with plasma renin activity suppressed (reports to follow in the chart).

Impression: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) - hypertension resistant to three agents, spontaneous-range hypokalemia on supplementation, high-normal sodium, elevated aldosterone with low renin, and a family history of the same disorder.

Plan: continue current antihypertensives and potassium chloride 40 mEq twice daily. Return to this clinic in 6 months with repeat electrolytes and renin/aldosterone.

Allergies reviewed: NKDA.
Outside endocrinology

documents.title: Endocrine visit
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Did you get the letter from the endocrinologist? She said it's the adrenal thing like my aunt. I'm not totally sure what happens next, they said to come back in 6 months.

documents.title: RE: Endocrine visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Got it and read it. The tests show your adrenal glands are making too much aldosterone, a hormone that holds on to salt and pushes out potassium - which fits both your blood pressure and your low potassium. Endocrinology is leading on this; their plan for now is to keep your current medicines and potassium and recheck in 6 months. Keep sending me your home readings and keep your fall physical with me.

Impression: primary hyperaldosteronism with persistent hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.

Plan: continue the present regimen. Follow up with primary care for blood pressure and potassium monitoring.

documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE GASTROENTEROLOGY - NEW CONSULTATION
Date of visit: 03/19/2024
Reason: chronic watery diarrhea, referred by primary care.

Ms. Nowak, 46, has known primary hyperaldosteronism followed by endocrinology. For several weeks she has had large-volume watery stools that keep coming even on days she fasts. She has cramping in her legs and hands and gets lightheaded. Stool infectious studies, celiac serology and TSH from her PCP were negative. Colonoscopy 06/2023 was normal.

Medications: lisinopril 20 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, potassium chloride 40 mEq twice daily, pantoprazole 40 mg.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: father hypertension, ruptured cerebral aneurysm at 67; mother type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia; paternal aunt with primary hyperaldosteronism.
Social: never smoker, rare wine, self-employed landscaper.

Exam: dry mucous membranes and decreased skin turgor; she looks volume depleted. Abdomen soft, nontender, no masses.

Labs today: potassium 2.0 mEq/L, venous pH 7.30, glucose 150 mg/dL (non-fasting). Stool electrolytes give a low osmotic gap (resulted 03/20).

Addendum 03/19 16:50: potassium of 2.0 called to the patient; she was sent to the hospital infusion unit this evening for intravenous potassium chloride with cardiac monitoring and went home afterward. Her primary care office is asked to repeat a BMP later this week.

Assessment: secretory diarrhea - persists with fasting, low stool osmotic gap - with severe hypokalemia and acidosis from stool losses. Infection, celiac disease and microscopic colitis on a normal colonoscopy are less likely. A hormone-secreting neuroendocrine tumor needs to be excluded.

Plan: CT abdomen with a pancreatic protocol. Continue oral potassium and oral rehydration. Return after imaging.

Outside gastroenterology

conditions.label: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (VIPoma)
conditions.note: 3.1 cm pancreatic tail mass on CT; hormone confirmed later

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text:
Indication: secretory diarrhea, evaluate for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.
Technique: multiphase CT of the abdomen with pancreatic protocol (non-contrast, late arterial and portal venous phases) with portal venous imaging of the pelvis. 100 mL IV contrast.
Findings: In the pancreatic tail there is a 3.1 x 2.7 cm well-circumscribed mass that enhances avidly in the late arterial phase and becomes isodense on the portal venous phase. The pancreatic duct is not dilated. The remainder of the pancreas is normal. The splenic vein is patent. The liver is normal in size without focal lesions. Gallbladder, spleen and kidneys are normal. Adrenal glands are unremarkable. No lymphadenopathy. Small and large bowel are fluid-filled without wall thickening. No ascites. Pelvic organs are unremarkable.
Bones: no suspicious lesions.
reports.conclusion: 3.1 cm arterially enhancing pancreatic tail mass, most consistent with a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. No liver lesions or adenopathy.

reports.text:
Specimen: distal pancreas, laparoscopic spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy.
Gross: segment of distal pancreas 9.0 x 3.5 x 3.0 cm containing a well-circumscribed tan-pink mass, 3.1 cm in greatest dimension.
Microscopic: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with nested and trabecular growth. Mitoses fewer than 2 per 2 mm2. Ki-67 proliferation index 2%. Immunohistochemistry: synaptophysin and chromogranin positive; vasoactive intestinal peptide positive.
Margins: pancreatic transection and peripancreatic soft tissue margins negative. Lymphovascular invasion not identified.
Lymph nodes: 0 of 8 involved.
reports.conclusion: Well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, WHO grade 1 (Ki-67 2%), 3.1 cm, VIP immunostain positive, margins negative, 0/8 nodes.

REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER - SURGICAL ONCOLOGY DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 11/19/2024, discharged 11/23/2024.

Diagnosis: pancreatic tail neuroendocrine tumor (VIPoma).
Procedure 11/19: laparoscopic spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy. Estimated blood loss minimal. Drain placed.
Other problems: primary hyperaldosteronism with resistant hypertension, chronic hypokalemia, peptic ulcer disease.

Course: uneventful. Diet advanced by day 2. Drain amylase low and drain removed on day 3. Potassium replaced intravenously the first night, then her home oral dose resumed. Pathology: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, grade 1, 3.1 cm, Ki-67 2%, VIP positive, margins negative, 0/8 nodes.

Discharge medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, potassium chloride 40 mEq twice daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, oxycodone-acetaminophen 5/325 one tablet every 6 hours as needed (12 tablets). Octreotide discontinued.

Follow-up: surgical oncology clinic 2 weeks; VIP level at 3 months; surveillance imaging at 1 year; PCP within 2 weeks.

REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER - EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD
Date of visit: 09/15/2025

CC: vomiting.
HPI: 47-year-old woman with primary hyperaldosteronism, a resected pancreatic VIPoma and a history of peptic ulcer disease, with two days of severe nausea and vomiting many times a day. She cannot keep down food or fluids. For the past few weeks she has also had intermittent epigastric pain. No diarrhea, no blood in the vomit, no fever.
Meds: lisinopril 20, amlodipine 10, hydrochlorothiazide 25, potassium chloride 40 mEq BID, pantoprazole 40.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP 100/60, HR 110. Dry mucous membranes, looks dehydrated. Abdomen soft, mild epigastric tenderness, no guarding, no distension.

Labs: Na 140, K 2.9, Cl 90, HCO3 32, BUN 28, Cr 1.0. Urine chloride 10 mEq/L. Lipase normal. CBC and magnesium normal.

ED course: 2 L normal saline with 20 mEq KCl per liter, ondansetron 4 mg IV, pantoprazole 40 mg IV. Nausea settled; tolerated crackers and fluids; oral potassium chloride 40 mEq given. Repeat HR 88, BP 124/78.

Impression: hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis from vomiting, with hypovolemia and dehydration; hypokalemia, taking oral replacement and tolerating it.
Disposition: home. Ondansetron 4 mg ODT every 8 hours as needed. Continue home medications. PCP within 2-3 days and GI follow-up for the epigastric pain. Return for persistent vomiting, blood, black stool or worsening pain.

HPI: 48-year-old woman with primary hyperaldosteronism and a resected pancreatic VIPoma, who has had chronic headaches and recurrent low potassium. About an hour before arrival, while working in a garden bed, she had an abrupt, severe headache - the worst she has ever had - with a stiff neck and light hurting her eyes. No trauma. No loss of consciousness reported.
Meds: lisinopril, amlodipine 10 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, potassium chloride 40 mEq BID, pantoprazole 40 mg.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: father died of a ruptured cerebral aneurysm at 67.

Exam: BP 158/94, HR 102, T 37.2 C (99 F). Awake and alert but anxious. Nuchal rigidity. Pupils equal and reactive, cranial nerves intact, strength and sensation symmetric - no focal deficit. GCS 15.

Noncontrast head CT: acute subarachnoid blood around the brainstem and in the basal cisterns.

Impression: acute subarachnoid hemorrhage, presumed aneurysmal.
Plan: neurosurgery and neurocritical care consulted; blood pressure lowered with IV nicardipine; CT angiography; admit to neuro ICU.

documents.title: Discharge Summary - Neurocritical Care
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER - DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 03/26/2026. Discharged 04/09/2026.

Principal diagnosis: aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured basilar tip aneurysm.
Other: primary hyperaldosteronism with resistant hypertension; chronic hypokalemia; resected pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (VIPoma); peptic ulcer disease.
Allergies: NKDA.

Presentation: sudden worst-ever headache while gardening, neck stiffness and photophobia; BP 158/94, HR 102; nuchal rigidity without focal deficit. Head CT showed subarachnoid blood around the brainstem and basal cisterns.

Course:
- CT angiography 03/26: 7 mm aneurysm at the basilar tip; no other aneurysm.
- Endovascular coil embolization the night of 03/26 via right femoral access, with complete occlusion of the aneurysm. No complications.
- Neuro ICU: nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours started on admission for a 21-day course. Blood pressure controlled with IV nicardipine, then her home lisinopril, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. Daily neuro checks and transcranial ultrasound showed no vasospasm. No hydrocephalus. Potassium replaced as needed in addition to her home dose.
- Moved to the neuroscience floor on day 9; walking independently; headache improving on scheduled acetaminophen.

Discharge exam: alert, oriented, fluent; no focal deficit.

Discharge medications: nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours through 04/15/2026, then stop; lisinopril 20 mg daily; amlodipine 10 mg daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; potassium chloride 40 mEq twice daily; pantoprazole 40 mg daily.
Instructions: no driving or heavy lifting until cleared by neurosurgery; return for new severe headache, weakness, confusion or seizure.
Follow-up: PCP within 1 week; neurosurgery clinic in 4 weeks; follow-up angiography about 6 months after coiling.

S: Headache easing, 1-3/10, acetaminophen once a day. Tired, napping. Neck less stiff. Finished nimodipine yesterday. No weakness, numbness, speech or vision problems. Eating fine. Groin site healed.
Meds: lisinopril 20, amlodipine 10, HCTZ 25, KCl 40 BID, pantoprazole 40. Nimodipine completed. NKDA.
O: BP as recorded. Alert, oriented, conversant. CN II-XII intact, strength 5/5 throughout, sensation and gait normal. Neck supple. Heart RRR. R groin no hematoma or bruit.
A/P
1. SAH from ruptured basilar aneurysm, s/p coiling - neurologically intact. Neurosurgery clinic 5/7; angiogram ~6 mo. No driving until neurosurgery clears.
2. Resistant HTN / primary hyperaldosteronism - BP 148/92, too high after an aneurysm bleed. Home log BID for 4 wks and bring it; we'll decide on the regimen at the next visit with neurosurgery input. BMP today.
3. Hypokalemia - continue 40 BID.
